name: Hāngi (Māori Earth Oven)
description: Traditional earth oven of the Māori, in which volcanic stones are heated in a pit, food is laid on the stones, and the oven is covered with leaves and earth to steam the meal. The hāngi cooks meat and vegetables by the heat of the stones, and it remains a central feature of hui and celebration, its method passed down through generations.
source: Ethnographic records of Māori cooking traditions

name: Kundu Drum
description: Hourglass hand drum of Papua New Guinea, carved from a single block of wood with a membrane of lizard or snake skin stretched over one head. The kundu is played with the palm and fingers to accompany sing-sing and dance, and in many communities it is the voice of the spirits, its patterns of beats belonging to the village and its ancestors.
material: wood, lizard or snake skin, resin
source: Ethnomusicological studies of Melanesian music

name: Bilum (Loop String Bag)
description: Woven looped-string bag of Papua New Guinea, made by women from plant fibre in a continuous spiral of loops. The bilum is carried over the head or shoulder for tools and produce, holds infants in the highlands, and is also made as a treasured ceremonial piece, its patterns and colours carrying the identity of the clan.
source: Ethnographic records of Highlands material culture

name: Trobriand Yam House (Bwaima)
description: Ornate storehouse of the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea, raised on posts with a steeply pitched roof and decorative woven friezes. The bwaima stores yams, the central wealth and prestige crop, and a man's status is read in the size and beauty of his yam house, which is built to display abundance as the symbolic face of his household.
source: Anthropological studies of the Trobriand Islands

name: Vanuatu Slit Drum (Tamtam)
description: Hollowed log drum of Vanuatu, carved from a single tree trunk with a narrow slot and open ends, struck with beaters to send sound across the village and reef. The slit drum calls people to gatherings, marks the rhythm of dances, and in the northern islands the great carved tamtam stand before the village as monumental records of chiefs.
maker: Vanuatuan carvers of the northern islands
source: Ethnographic accounts of Vanuatuan music and carving

name: Tabua (Whale Tooth)
description: Polished sperm whale tooth of Fiji, presented at weddings, funerals and reconciliation as the highest mark of respect and goodwill. The tabua is offered with a formal speech and is kept by the recipient to seal the covenant, and its giving seals covenants between chiefs, so that a request carried with a tabua is rarely refused.
source: Ethnographic studies of Fijian ceremonial exchange

name: Fijian Masi (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Fiji, beaten from the inner bark of the paper mulberry and painted with geometric designs in black and brown. Masi is made by women for gifts, ceremony and dress, and the finest pieces are given at weddings and installed in the chiefly house, where their patterns record the clan and its history.
source: Ethnographic records of Fijian material culture

name: Fijian War Club
description: Carved club of the Fijian islands, shaped in a range of forms from long straight blades to bulbous knobs, and often ornamented with incised patterns. War clubs were the emblem of the Fijian warrior and were also used as badges of rank, passed down as trophies and treasures, with some weapons bearing a name and the history of their owners.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Fijian weaponry

name: Solomon Islands Shell Money
description: Traditional currency of the Solomon Islands, made from small discs ground from shell and strung on fibre in long coils. Shell money is still used in bride-price, compensation and chiefly exchange, its value fixed by the species of shell and the skill of its making, and the red feather-money of the Reef Islands is among the most prized forms.
source: Ethnographic studies of Solomon Islands economy

name: Hawaiian Feather Cloak (ʻAhuʻula)
description: Royal cloak of the Hawaiian chiefs, built on a netted fibre base and covered with hundreds of thousands of small yellow, red and black feathers from native birds such as the ʻōʻō and mamo. The ʻahuʻula was the mark of the highest aliʻi, each cloak taking generations of birds to complete, and it was worn in war and ceremony as a living symbol of chiefly mana.
maker: Hawaiian feather workers of the chiefly courts
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Hawaiian regalia

name: Lei Niho Palaoa (Whale-Tooth Pendant)
description: Pendant of the Hawaiian chiefs made from a carved sperm whale tooth suspended on a braid of human hair, worn by men and women of high rank. The lei niho palaoa was a sign of royalty and genealogical status, and it was forbidden to anyone beneath the chiefly class; the hair cord was itself a gift of honour between the wearer and its giver.
material: sperm whale tooth, braided human hair
maker: Hawaiian craftsmen of the chiefly class
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Hawaiian adornment

name: Hawaiian Pahu (Drum)
description: Standing drum of the Hawaiian islands, carved from a single log of coconut or breadfruit wood with a head of sharkskin stretched and braced with cord. The pahu is struck with the hands to accompany hula and ceremony, and in the heiau it was a sacred instrument whose rhythms called the gods and marked the rites of the temple.
material: coconut or breadfruit wood, sharkskin, fibre cord
source: Ethnomusicological studies of Hawaiian music

name: Samoan Siapo (Tapa)
description: Barkcloth of Samoa, beaten from the inner bark of the paper mulberry into large sheets and painted or printed with geometric patterns in earth tones. Siapo is made by women for wrapping, dress and ceremony, and its designs are handed down within families, each district owning particular patterns that mark the cloth as its own.
source: Ethnographic records of Samoan material culture

name: Samoan ʻIe Toga (Fine Mat)
description: Treasured fine mat of Samoa, woven from the thinnest strips of pandanus by senior women and polished with oil to a fine sheen. The ʻie toga is the highest form of Samoan wealth, exchanged at weddings, funerals and political occasions, and the oldest mats are given names and genealogies and counted among the most sacred possessions of the family.
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Samoan ceremonial exchange

name: Samoan Tātau Tools
description: Set of combs and mallets used in the Samoan tatau, the traditional hand-tapped tattoo applied by a tufuga ta tatau. A comb of bone or turtle shell set with teeth is dipped in soot pigment and struck with a wooden mallet to drive ink into the skin, a practice preserved by legend from the goddesses Taema and Tilafaiga, who brought the art from Fiti.
material: bone, turtle shell, wood, soot pigment
source: Ethnographic accounts of Samoan tattooing; oral tradition

name: Tongan Ngatu (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of Tonga, made by beating the inner bark of the hiapo tree and pasting the strips together into large sheets painted with stencil patterns in brown and black. Ngatu is produced by women in working parties and given at weddings, funerals and royal ceremonies, and the largest ceremonial pieces are presented to the king.
source: Ethnographic records of Tongan material culture

name: Tahitian Vaʻa (Outrigger Canoe)
description: Ocean-going sailing canoe of the Tahitians, built with a single outrigger float and a lateen sail of matting that carried voyagers across the Pacific. The vaʻa was the vessel of the great Polynesian navigators, who read the stars and swells to settle islands, and it remains raced in the sport of vaʻa today, each hull shaped with the inherited knowledge of the builders.
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Polynesian voyaging

name: Marquesan War Club (Uʻu)
description: Polished war club of the Marquesas Islands, carved from ironwood with a long shaft and a flattened head, sometimes inlaid with the teeth of the whale or the bones of enemies. The uʻu was the principal weapon of the Marquesan warrior and was also a treasured gift, its elaborate carving a record of the man who bore it and his ancestry.
source: Ethnographic accounts of Marquesan weaponry

name: Cook Islands Adze (Toki)
description: Stone-bladed adze of the Cook Islands, ground from basalt and lashed to a wooden handle, used to fell and shape the timber for canoes, houses and carvings. The toki was the essential tool of the master craftsman, and finely made adzes were treasured and handed down, with the stone sources on the islands prized and controlled by chiefly families.
material: basalt stone, wooden handle, fibre lashing
source: Archaeological and ethnographic records of Cook Islands technology

name: Marshall Islands Stick Chart
description: Navigation chart of the Marshall Islands built from pandanus ribs and coconut fibre, with cowrie shells marking islands and the curved sticks recording the pattern of ocean swells. Read by trained navigators before a voyage, the charts encode the wave and current knowledge of the Pacific, and the same skill guided the first navigators across the atolls.
material: pandanus ribs, coconut fibre, cowrie shells
source: Ethnographic scholarship on Marshallese navigation

name: Yap Stone Money (Rai)
description: Large circular discs of quarried calcite used as currency on the island of Yap, some measuring several metres across and weighing tonnes. Rai were quarried on Palau and sailed back to Yap, their value fixed not by size alone but by the difficulty of the voyage and the lives lost in obtaining them, and ownership was remembered rather than physically moved.
source: Anthropological studies of Yapese economy

name: Palau Storyboard
description: Carved wooden panel of Palau recording the myths and histories of the island in low-relief figures. The gables of the bai, the men's meeting house, bore painted frieze boards recording village legend, and from the twentieth century the stories came to be carved in low-relief wood as the celebrated storyboards.
maker: Palauan carvers of the bai tradition
source: Ethnographic records of Palauan art and architecture

name: Nan Madol (Basalt City)
description: Ruined city of the island of Pohnpei built on artificial islets from great basalt columns, the ceremonial and political centre of the Saudeleur dynasty. Legend holds that the walls were raised by magic, and the city fell to the warrior Isokelekel, who came from the east and overthrew the Saudeleurs, so that Nan Madol endures as the greatest monument of Micronesia.
source: Archaeological and historical studies of Nan Madol

name: Hawaiian Kapa (Barkcloth)
description: Barkcloth of the Hawaiian islands, beaten from the inner bark of the wauke tree and printed with geometric designs by stamping with carved blocks and leaves. Kapa was made by women for clothing, bedding and ritual, and the finest pieces were kept by the chiefs, their patterns bearing the mana of the maker and the household.
source: Ethnographic records of Hawaiian material culture

name: Tuvaluan Paopao (Fishing Canoe)
description: Small sailing canoe of the Tuvaluan islands, fitted with a single outrigger and a triangular sail, used for fishing on the lagoon and the open reef. The paopao was built by hand from the island timbers and lashed with sennit, and its design was carried across the atolls by the same navigational knowledge that tied the Pacific peoples together.
source: Ethnographic records of Tuvaluan seafaring

name: Kryždirbystė Cross
description: Carved oak wayside crosses of the Lithuanian cross-crafting tradition, one to five metres tall with small roofs and carved ornament. Once consecrated by a priest, a cross is sacred: set at village entrances, cemeteries and shrines, it draws offerings of food, rosaries, scarves and aprons seeking fertility or protection. The craft became a symbol of national identity under Russian and Soviet rule.
source: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Cross-crafting and its symbolism (2001); LNKC Savadas (Lithuanian National Culture Centre)

name: Lietuviška Juosta
description: Hand-woven linen and woollen sash, rich with geometric patterns, worn by Lithuanian men and women with festive dress and given as gifts at weddings, christenings and funerals. The symbol system is protective: the sash binds, fastens and marks a sacred boundary, and folk belief made the woven band a mediator, even an offering, between people and mythical beings.
source: Ethnographic studies of Lithuanian sash symbolism (Lietuvių juostų simbolika, Lituanistika)

name: Verbos Easter Palms
description: Tall bouquets of dried and dyed grasses, flowers, juniper and willow bound onto a nut-tree rod, carried to church on Palm Sunday for consecration and kept in an honoured place at home. The verba tradition, practised for at least seven generations in villages northwest of Vilnius, is recorded in paintings and ethnographies since the mid-1800s and still marks Easter and the St. Casimir's fair.
material: dried and dyed grasses, flowers, juniper, willow, hazel rod
source: LNKC Savadas: The tradition of tying verbos (Easter palms) in Vilnius region; documentary records since Kanutas Ruseckas (1847) and Oscar Kolberg (1866)

name: Kanklės
description: Archaic Lithuanian plucked box zither, a trapezoid of solid wood strung with parallel strings, of the same Baltic psaltery family as the Latvian kokle and Estonian kannel. Old belief held that bards (vaidilos) sang heroic songs and served the gods to its music, and that the best instrument wood was cut between a person's death and funeral — a mourned person lent the kanklės a sorrowful voice.
material: maple, linden or ash wood, wire or gut strings
source: LNKC survey of Lithuanian string instruments (chordophones); Lithuanian ethnomusicology

name: Eglė's Dress
description: In the Lithuanian tale 'Eglė the Queen of Serpents', the clothes Eglė wore when bathing at the lake — a coiled grass snake slipped into her sleeve and would return her clothing only if she promised to marry its king. That pledged garment drives the tale: nine years under the sea, three impossible tasks, and Eglė's lasting transformation into a spruce tree.
source: Lithuanian folk tale 'Eglė žalčių karalienė'; first translation printed 1837 by M. Jasevičius, recorded in Lithuanian folklore collections

name: Lielvārde Belt
description: The Lielvārde belt: a wide woven wool sash of red-and-white geometric patterns worn with Latvian folk costume, from central Latvia's Lielvārde region. Legendary as a protective band said to ward off evil, it has since the 1970s been read as a code of the universe and human DNA. Janīna Kursīte traces its red-white symbolism to ancient protective clothing and incantations.
maker: Latvian village weavers of the Lielvārde region
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Lielvārdas josta (2008); folklore researcher Janīna Kursīte

name: Sakta Brooch
description: The sakta, the ancient Baltic breast brooch of bronze, silver or silver-gilt, fastened the folk costume — especially the bride's — at throat or chest. Archaeological finds date the fibula type back two millennia; the later 'bubble' saktas with hemispherical bosses and glass eyes were trusted as savings. A Latvian folk song says goddess Laima makes fibulae for a girl, 'immersing them in silver'.
source: Latvijas Banka, Gold Brooches: The Bubble Fibula; Latvian archaeological and ethnographic collections

name: Kokle
description: The Latvian plucked box zither: a trapezoid soundbox with parallel strings over a flat board. A document of 1225, when chronicler Henricus de Lettis mentioned it, makes the kokle the oldest documented psaltery in Europe. Latvian folk songs call its strings 'silver war' and 'golden war'. The kokle and the art of koklēšana were placed in the Latvian Cultural Canon in 2008 as the national instrument.
material: maple or ash wood, metal strings
source: Latvijas Kultūras kanons: Kokles un koklēšana (2008); Henricus de Lettis (1225)

name: Laima's Distaff
description: The distaff of fate in Latvian and Lithuanian belief: a carved spindle-holder on which the goddess Laima, or the forest fairy Lauma, spinning thread, fixes the length and luck of a human life. Folk accounts describe laumas borrowing distaffs and spindles from village women and spinning linen by night. The distaff stands for fate's measuring thread in Latvian spinning dainas.
source: Latvian and Lithuanian folklore accounts of Laima and laumas as spinners of fate (Latvian dainas; Britannica: Laima)

name: Jāņi Wreath
description: The midsummer wreath of Jāņi: for women and girls, plaited from flowers, grasses and herbs — a braid of twenty-seven plants was held to ward off disasters, disease and enemies — while men and boys wore rings of oak leaves as symbols of strength. Worn through Līgo night on 23 June with singing and bonfire jumping, the wreath is kept afterwards for protection and healing.
source: Latvian Jāņi folklore; midsummer customs documented since Paul Einhorn (1627)

name: Estonian Kannel
description: Estonia's plucked box zither, a small winged or trapezoid instrument of carved wood strung with wire or gut strings, played to accompany regilaul, the ancient runic-song tradition shared with Finland's kantele and Lithuania's kanklės. Regilaul texts and folk archaeology show the kannel in Baltic-Finnic music for over a millennium, and it remains central to Estonian folk revival ensembles.
material: carved wood, wire or gut strings
source: Estonian folk music scholarship; Estonian National Museum instrument collections

name: Seto Folk Costume
description: The Seto women's folk costume of south-eastern Estonia's Setomaa: a striking white, black and red ensemble of striped or checked skirt, linen blouse, woven belt and silver jewellery, worn for leelo singing, church feasts and Seto Kingdom Day. The costume is integral to the Seto polyphonic leelo tradition inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, in which choirs sang in traditional dress.
source: UNESCO: Seto Leelo, Seto polyphonic singing tradition (2009); Visit Setomaa ethnographic accounts

name: Kihnu Woolen Skirt
description: The striped woolen skirt and knitted garments of Kihnu Island's women: bright red, green and blue striped cloth woven on home looms from local wool, worn with embroidered blouses, sashes, mittens and stockings whose colours and patterns recall old legends. Kihnu's women, keeping the island's culture while men were at sea, made these garments the emblem of the UNESCO-listed Kihnu cultural space.
source: UNESCO: Kihnu cultural space (2003); Kihnu women's handicraft tradition

name: Kirivöö Belt
description: The kirivöö, the Estonian pick-up patterned belt: a narrow woven band of wool over linen thread carrying rows of small crosses, rhombuses, triangles and diagonal figures, worn by women with folk dress. The Estonian National Museum holds belts from across the country; regional edge patterns distinguish parishes, and the belts served as gifts, love-pledges and protective charms.
source: Studia Vernacula: 'Small patterns at the edges of belts' (Estonian National Museum, 2018)

name: Põhjanael
description: The Põhjanael, the 'North Nail', the Estonian folk name for the North Star: in the old Baltic-Finnic worldview the sky was an upturned cauldron or great wheel turning on a nail driven through it, and that nail is Polaris. Farmers read seasons from the stars around it. Folklorist Matthias Johann Eisen recorded the motif in his 'Eesti Mütoloogia' and folk astronomy notes.
source: M. J. Eisen, Eesti Mütoloogia IV; Estonian folk astronomy tradition
